name: Scan the mailbox for new replies, headers only
description: THE OUTLOOK HALF OF THE REPLY-DRAFTING AGENT. It is the Gmail plan step for step, decision for decision, and the only differences are the ones Graph forces: every one of them is named where it occurs, so the two files can be read side by side and any real divergence stands out. THE FIRST THING THAT HAPPENS, and nothing about any client is read before it. HEADERS ONLY, AND THAT IS THE PRIVACY DESIGN, not a saving. Scanning before anyone knows who is a client means this pass sees whatever arrived — the owner's accountant, their landlord, a newsletter — so what it is allowed to fetch has to be the narrowest thing that still identifies a sender. `metadata` is exactly that: addresses, subject and a preview, and no body. A non-client's actual words are therefore never pulled into the run at all. The body is fetched in step 6, after the sender is confirmed to be somebody this business has written to. DIFFERENCE: the window is `within_days` rather than Gmail's `newer_than:Nd` query. Graph has no date syntax in a free-text search, and it REFUSES a message request carrying both `$search` and `$filter`, so a window has to be a filter — and it has to be expressed in days, because the only thing that knows the window is `planInputs`, which derives it from the agent's own cadence. `{{input.scan_days}}` is the ONLY thing defining 'new', and it carries a day of slack for a failed run, so a reply can surface on two consecutive runs; step 7b is what stops that becoming two drafts.

name: Read the service list
description: After the scan, so a business whose clients all stayed quiet reads nothing. Once per run rather than once per reply, because it is the same answer for everybody. This is the only business fact the agent gets beyond one client's own correspondence, and everything it refuses later traces back to that being deliberately short: a price on a published service is already public, so repeating it to the person who asked commits the owner to nothing. Identical to the Gmail plan — the business side of this agent does not know which mailbox it is reading.

name: Work each message that came in
description: ONE PERSON'S FAILURE MUST NOT STOP THE REST, so `continueOnError` is set. A failing scatter item otherwise re-throws and aborts the whole run, and per-item failures are ordinary here: a search that throttles, a body the model will not classify, a draft that will not save. The loop runs over MESSAGES, so each inbound mail is considered exactly once per run however many letters the business sent that person.

steps.name: Ask what we have sent this sender
steps.description:
THE FILTER AND THE HISTORY ARE ONE QUESTION, which is why this is a single read rather than an existence check followed by a fetch. 'What has this business sent to this address?' answers both: the rows ARE the history the model needs, and no rows means this business has never written to them, so the message is none of the agent's business. Matching on `email_sends.to_email` rather than on a contact is deliberate: somebody in the CRM we have never emailed cannot be replying to us, and a reply to our own mail is the only thing this agent is for. `from_email` means the same bare lowercase address on both providers — on Outlook it is an alias, because Graph already hands back a structured address, where Gmail reads a MIME header and has to parse `"Dana Levi" <dana@host>` out of it. One name, one meaning, whichever mailbox answered.

EITHER ADDRESS THE REPLY CARRIES, because a client replying is not obliged to reply AS the address we wrote to. A Microsoft 365 account answers through its tenant relay, so a mail sent to `someone@their-domain.com` comes back From `someone@tenant.onmicrosoft.com` — Gmail renders it as 'via <tenant>.onmicrosoft.com'. Matching the send log on `from_email` alone found nothing, so a real client with eight prior sends was read as a stranger: the gate closed, the escalation had no contact to attach to, and `activities.create` refused the write that was supposed to reach the owner.

`reply_to_email` is the address that relay sets back to the human, and the mail executors already extract it. Matching on both is strictly wider and cannot admit anybody new: a row only exists in `email_sends` if THIS business sent to that address with a contact attached.

FIVE ROWS, NOT TEN. The gate needs only `count`; the prompt needs only enough to recognise what a reply is ABOUT, and five subjects establish a relationship that ten do not establish harder.

steps.name: Only go on if this is a reply to our own mail
steps.description: THE BOUNDARY, and the cheapest gate in the run: an integer compared to zero, before any body is fetched, before the model is called, before anything is written. `count` is guaranteed on every business-os find result. Anything from an address with no send history stops dead here and only its headers were ever read. `contact_id is_not_null` on the find above is the second half of the same guard: a NULL contact on `email_sends` means the mail went to the OWNER rather than a client (a briefing, a dispute alert), so a reply to one of those is the owner's own correspondence and must not qualify either.

steps.name: Now fetch what they actually wrote
steps.description: THE ONLY PLACE A BODY IS FETCHED, and it is inside the boundary gate on purpose: by here the sender is known to be somebody this business has written to, so no stranger's words are ever pulled down. DIFFERENCE: `from_address` is an exact OData filter where Gmail used a `from:` search term — which is the better instrument anyway, and the only one available alongside the date window. Searching by sender rather than by message id because neither mail plugin has a get-by-id action. That cannot fetch the 'wrong' message in any way that matters: it returns the newest mail from this person inside the same window the scan used, and the newest is what the agent wants to answer regardless of which one the scan happened to surface. Full content here, where step 1 took headers only, because a 255-character preview truncates mid-question and the whole run exists to read what was asked. `body` is the readable text on this provider as well as on Gmail — it used to be populated only for a plaintext message, which almost no business email is, so the model would have been handed nothing to read and would have escalated every single message.

steps.name: What was last sent to this client from this mailbox
steps.description: The sent folder rather than the send log, because the thing worth knowing is whether the OWNER has already answered from their own mail client, and nothing they type in Outlook reaches `email_sends`. Only the latest is fetched: the model is asked whether it answers the reply, not to audit a thread. This exists because at a daily rhythm the owner has usually dealt with it themselves, and a drafts folder full of answers to settled questions is how an owner stops trusting this agent. TWO DIFFERENCES, both Graph's: the folder is `sentitems`, not `sent`; and the recipient is matched with `to_address`, because in this folder and the next the SENDER is always the owner, so `from_address` would match everything and answer nothing. `metadata` rather than Gmail's `snippet` — Outlook has two content levels where Gmail has three, and `metadata` already carries the preview this step wants.

steps.name: Have we already drafted one for them?
steps.description: SCOPED TO THIS CONVERSATION, not to this person. It asked whether ANY draft to this client was waiting, and stopped the whole message if one was — no classification, no label, no row, nothing to look at. So one unrelated draft sitting in the folder silenced that client completely for two days. Measured on 2026-11-15: a client wrote "I don't understand why you charged me if I couldn't make the appointment", the agent read it, marked it read and stopped here, because a draft about something else was open. That was tolerable when the only outcome was another draft. It is not now: the thing being dropped is a client who would have been answered automatically, and it is dropped in silence. A draft on THIS thread is a real reason to hold off; a draft to the same person about a different booking is not. It fails OPEN by design — a subject that breaks the search returns nothing, `total_found` is 0, and the message is classified rather than silently held. Outlook takes `subject_prefix` as its own parameter rather than a query string, so there is nothing to quote and nothing to escape. THE MEMORY, and it is the owner's own drafts folder rather than a table. The scan window is two days so a run that failed loses nothing, which means a reply can be seen on two consecutive mornings — and without this the second morning writes a second draft of the same answer. A draft we wrote is the record that we wrote it: it sits in `drafts` addressed to that client until the owner does something with it. SELF-CLEARING, which is why this beats a stored flag. Send the draft and it leaves `drafts` for `sentitems`, where step 7 finds it and the model answers `already_handled`. Discard it and the next run writes a fresh one, which is the right behaviour — the owner threw the first away. It works identically on both providers because both file a draft under the recipient it is addressed to, which is the only property this depends on.

steps.name: Only think about it if none is waiting
steps.description: Gated BEFORE the model, so a second sighting of the same reply costs an integer comparison rather than a model call. `total_found` is the name Gmail uses and Outlook now reports it too, for the same reason `from_email` is aliased: a gate on how many messages came back should read one key whichever mailbox answered, or the same condition means two things in two files and only one of them was ever tested.

steps.name: Decide what becomes of this reply
steps.description: THE ORDER OF THE RULES IS THE WHOLE DESIGN, and it was wrong once. `needs_owner` said "choose this when answering would need any fact you were not given" — which is ALWAYS true of a refund, so it swallowed `send_link` every time. Measured 2026-11-15: the model correctly wrote "the client is asking for a refund" and then escalated anyway, reasoning that it did not know the policy. It was obeying the rules it was given. So the doors are now read FIRST, and both definitions say the same thing from their own side: not knowing the answer is the reason to send a door, never a reason to escalate. A door collects what is missing; `needs_owner` is for what no page can. THE SAME PROMPT AS THE GMAIL PLAN, WORD FOR WORD, and that is deliberate. The judgement an agent makes about a client's message cannot depend on which mail provider the owner happens to use; two prompts that drifted apart would mean one owner's agent escalates what another's answers, with nothing to point at. FOUR OUTCOMES, NOT A YES OR NO, and the two refusals are not the same refusal. An out-of-office and a client asking to move an appointment both mean 'cannot answer', but one deserves the owner's attention and the other deserves silence; collapsing them means either every bounce interrupts the owner or real escalations get swallowed in the noise. `already_handled` is the fourth, and it is a judgement rather than a date comparison on purpose: asking whether our last message answers their question is both sturdier and more useful than asking whether it arrived afterwards. REFUSING IS THE DEFAULT. The draft reaches the owner, never the client, so a refusal costs one glance and a confident wrong answer costs a client.
steps.prompt:
You are the front desk of a small business, drafting a reply for the OWNER to read and send. You never send anything yourself, and the client never hears from you directly.

THE MESSAGE THAT JUST ARRIVED
  from: {{current_reply.from}}
  subject: {{current_reply.subject}}
  message: {{full_message.emails.0.body}}

WHAT THIS BUSINESS HAS SENT THIS PERSON BEFORE (newest first)
{{client_history.rows}}

THE LAST THING SENT TO THEM FROM THIS MAILBOX
{{our_last_word.emails}}

THE BUSINESS'S SERVICES — the only business facts you have
{{service_list.rows}}

If the message above is empty or missing, choose 'needs_owner' with the reason 'could not read the message' and write nothing. Never answer a message you cannot see.

Choose exactly ONE outcome.

Read these in order. The first one that fits is the answer, and the doors come
first on purpose: a page that collects what is missing beats interrupting the
owner, every time.

'send_link' — a page they can use themselves answers this. Choose it and name the `door`.

SENDING A DOOR IS NOT ANSWERING. This is the outcome for exactly the case where you do NOT know enough to reply: the page asks them which booking, which payment, how much and why, and it reaches the owner as a complete request instead of a conversation. You are not promising anything and you are not deciding anything.

So "I'd have to know the policy", "I'd have to know what they paid", "I'd have to know what was agreed" are all reasons to send a door — not reasons to escalate.

The doors:

  book        they want to book, or are asking what times you have.
              NEVER state availability yourself. The page shows what is free
              right now; a time you name may be gone by the time they read it.
  reschedule  they want to move an existing appointment.
  cancel      they want to cancel one.
  pay         they are asking how to pay, or for a payment link.
  intake      they are asking what you need from them before the appointment.
  quote       they are asking to see a quote again.
  refund      they are asking for MONEY BACK — a refund, a payment taken
              wrongly or twice, money back for something that did not happen.

Nothing you write is sent. The email is a fixed sentence and a button, chosen
by the door, so you are deciding WHERE to point them and nothing else.

One thing only is NOT a refund: asking what something costs. A published price you were
given is a 'draft'. Everything else about money already taken — asking for it back,
questioning a charge, "why was I charged", "I couldn't come and I was billed",
disputing an amount — is the refund door. They do not have to use the word refund.

If you are torn between 'send_link' and 'needs_owner', choose 'needs_owner'.
That is the older, safer path and it always reaches the owner.

'already_handled' — the last thing sent to them already answers what they are asking. Say nothing further. Choose this whenever it looks answered; a missed draft costs nothing and a duplicate one costs trust.

'ignore' — this needs no reply and the owner does not need to know. Out-of-office and holiday autoresponders, bounces, delivery and read receipts, unsubscribe confirmations, calendar notifications, and plain acknowledgements that ask nothing ('thanks!', 'great', 'noted'). Nothing is shown to the owner for these.

'needs_owner' — a question only the owner can answer, and NO page can collect.

Choose this when a PERSON has to decide or has to know something you do not. You do not know the diary, what this person owes or has paid, what was agreed in conversation, the address, the opening hours, or the business's policies.

BUT READ THE DOORS FIRST. If a page would collect what is missing, that page is the answer and you choose 'send_link'. "I would need to know the policy / the amount / what was decided" is a reason to send a door, never a reason to choose this.

Choose it for: complaints with no request attached; anything legal or medical; anything about another person's booking; a price that is not on the service list; a discount; something agreed in conversation. And choose it whenever no door fits and you are unsure. Unsure means needs_owner.

'draft' — you can answer completely from what you were given. Write the reply.

WHEN YOU CHOOSE 'draft', these rules are absolute:
1. Write in the SAME LANGUAGE the person wrote in. Never translate or transliterate their name.
2. State ONLY facts present above. Never invent or estimate a price, a duration, a date, a time, an address or a policy.
3. Never say or imply that anything is booked, held, confirmed, reserved or paid. Never promise a time.
4. Never apologise for something you cannot verify happened.
5. No links, no URLs.
6. Write as the business, first person, plainly. Three sentences at most.
7. No greeting and no sign-off — the owner's mail carries both.
8. Keep their subject, prefixed with 'Re: ' unless it already starts with it.
9. Answer the WHOLE message or choose needs_owner instead. Replying about the easy half of a two-part question and silently dropping the rest reads worse than not replying.

For 'quote': the client's OWN WORDS. Copy the one or two sentences from their message that say what they actually want — verbatim, in their language, at most 200 characters, trimmed at a sentence end. Do not translate it, do not summarise it and do not tidy their grammar. This is shown to the owner AS THE MESSAGE: it is the only part of the card that is the client speaking rather than you reporting, so an empty quote means the owner sees nothing of what was written and has to open their mailbox to find out. Strip greetings, sign-offs and any quoted earlier thread. Leave it empty only when the message itself is empty or unreadable.

For 'reason': one or two short sentences written for the OWNER, naming what was asked and what you would have needed. WRITE IT IN {{input.owner_language}}, WHICH IS THE OWNER'S OWN LANGUAGE — not the client's. This line is never sent to anybody; it appears on the owner's dashboard, and they are the only person who reads it.

The previous rule said to match the language the CLIENT wrote in, which has no answer when a message carries a Hebrew subject and an English body. Measured on 2026-11-10: the same message, processed twelve seconds apart, produced one English note and one Hebrew one. The draft reply still matches the client, because they read that one. This does not. Lead with what they actually asked for, in their words where you can, then what you would have needed to answer it. Write it as a note to a colleague, not a log line. Leave `subject` and `body` empty unless the outcome is 'draft'.

FOR 'needs_owner', ALSO WRITE A 'suggested_reply'. Same call, no second thought.

The owner is about to answer this person from their dashboard, and starting from
a blank box is the slowest part of the job. You cannot answer the question — that
is what 'needs_owner' MEANS — but you can write the holding reply they would
otherwise type themselves.

WHAT IT MAY SAY: that their message arrived, what you understood them to be
asking, and that the owner will come back to them. Nothing else.

WHAT IT MAY NEVER SAY, and this is absolute: no time, no date, no price, no
duration, no availability, no address, no policy, no promise that anything is
booked, held or confirmed. If you were not given a fact, it does not go in —
and for this outcome you were not given the fact that matters, or you would have
chosen 'draft'. Never apologise for something you cannot verify happened.

Write it in the SAME LANGUAGE THE PERSON WROTE IN — unlike 'reason', this one is
for THEM. Two sentences at most, no greeting and no sign-off, first person, as
the business.

A good one reads: "Thanks for letting me know — I understand you can't make that
time and would like a call about the service. I'll check and come straight back
to you." It commits to nothing and saves the owner the typing.

Leave `suggested_reply` empty for 'draft', 'ignore' and 'already_handled': the
first has a real reply in `body`, and the other two are not answered at all.

quote.description: The client's own words, verbatim, at most 200 characters.

suggested_reply.description: A holding reply for needs_owner. States no fact it was not given.

door.description: Required when outcome is 'send_link'. Which self-service page answers this message. Ignored otherwise.

steps.name: Draft it only when it chose to
steps.description: Gates on the chosen outcome rather than on a body being present. Told to refuse, a model will sometimes fill the other fields anyway out of helpfulness, and without this check that stray text would become a draft addressed to a real client.

steps.name: Leave the reply in the owner's drafts
steps.description: `create_draft` and nothing that sends — the agent writes to the owner's drafts folder and never to a client, and Outlook has no reply-and-send action at all. `reply_to_message_id` BUYS BACK THE THREADING WITHOUT THE SENDING, and this is the one place the two providers reach the same result by opposite routes. Gmail builds the reply and tells the API which conversation it joins. Graph exposes no threading field on a draft, so it is asked for a reply TO the message instead — `createReply` — and fills the rest in: the conversation, the recipient, the 'Re:' subject, and the original quoted beneath. Which is why NEITHER a recipient NOR a subject is passed here where the Gmail plan passes both: on this path Graph decides them from the message being answered, and passing our own would either be ignored (the subject) or override a correct answer with a guess. `{{decision.body}}` goes in as the owner's words, above the quote. Without any of this the draft was a separate message carrying 'Re:', which arrives beside the exchange it answers and reads, to the client, as a stranger to the thread they wrote in.

steps.name: Say so on the client's own timeline
steps.description: WITHOUT THIS THE AGENT IS INVISIBLE. A draft appears in the owner's Outlook with nothing in the platform saying where it came from, and the only record of a run lives in the execution's collected output, which nobody opens. The contact timeline is the surface an owner already reads when they ask what has happened with somebody, so the answer belongs there rather than in a screen built for this agent. It is also what the needs-you card reads, so this line is how a drafted reply reaches the owner's attention at all. `contact_id` comes from the send log read in step 4 — `email_sends` carries it, which is why that read is filtered on it being present. Non-blocking by position: the draft is already written by the time this runs, so a failure here costs the owner a line of history, not their reply.

steps.name: Show in the mailbox that a reply is waiting
steps.description: The Gmail twin labels the thread `AgentPilot/Drafted` so the owner can see the agent wrote something; this is the same mark as an Outlook category. NOT excluded by `step1`, deliberately: the drafts folder is the dedupe for this outcome (`step7b`, scoped to this conversation) and it is self-clearing. Send the draft and it leaves `drafts`, so `step7` finds it and the next read answers `already_handled`; discard it and the next run writes a fresh one, which is right, because the owner threw the first away. Excluding this category would turn a discarded draft into silence for ever.

steps.name: Or hand it to the owner
steps.description: `ignore` and `already_handled` doing nothing visible is correct — an out-of-office needs no reply and an answered question needs no second one — but `needs_owner` is the whole escalation, and silently dropping it would be worse than not classifying at all, because the owner believes the agent is watching their mail. It lands on the same timeline as a drafted reply, so one place answers both 'what did it do' and 'what does it need from me'.

steps.name: Note what they asked, and why it was left
steps.description: `reason` is already written for a person: the prompt asks for one short sentence addressed to the owner, naming what was asked and what the agent would have needed. So it goes in as written rather than being rephrased here. The subject is the title, because that is what the owner will recognise in a list of client history.

steps.name: Flag the message, since Outlook has no labels
steps.description:
THE OUTLOOK ANSWER TO GMAIL'S LABEL, AND NOW IT IS THE SAME ANSWER.

Two marks, doing two different jobs. High importance is the one the OWNER sees: a red marker beside the row, saying this one is waiting on them. The category is the one the AGENT sees, and it is what this plan previously had no way to write.

IT USED TO SAY THERE WAS NO EQUIVALENT. That was true of the three parameters this action exposed — read state, a folder move, an importance flag — and none of them can be filtered on safely: the owner sets importance for their own reasons, moving a client's mail takes it out of the inbox they are reading, and read state means 'somebody looked', which includes them. Filtering on any of those would skip the owner's own mail along with ours.

Graph has carried `categories` on a message all along; nothing exposed it. `modify_message` now takes `add_categories`, merging into whatever the owner already set rather than replacing it, and `search_emails` takes `exclude_categories`. So `step1` can skip what has been dealt with, exactly as the Gmail twin does with `-label:`, and the Outlook plan no longer leans on the watermark alone — which mattered, because the watermark cannot cover the ten-minute overlap, a manual run, or a failed run re-scanning its window up to five times.

steps.name: Or send them a page they can use themselves
steps.description: THE ONE OUTCOME THAT REACHES THE CLIENT, and the only send this agent has. It cannot carry a message: `send_portal_door_contacts` takes a DOOR from a closed list and the words come from a table, so the model decides where to point and never what to say. A door is a page where the CLIENT decides — a booking link does not book, a refund form does not refund — so a misread message costs them a door they do not walk through. NO MARKING STEP HERE, unlike the Gmail variant. Outlook has no labels in this plan — `step13b` flags an escalation with `importance: high` instead — so there is nothing to write and nothing for step 1 to exclude. The thread is not read again because `send_portal_door_contacts` refuses a second door to the same conversation, which lives in the action rather than the mailbox and therefore works for both providers.

steps.name: Send the page, or prepare it for the owner
steps.description: One action for every door. It reads `business_profiles.agents_may_reply_directly` at the point of sending, so no plan can bypass the owner's choice — including one written by hand. It also refuses to send the same door twice to one conversation.

steps.name: Mark the message, so it is not read again
steps.description:
THE OUTLOOK HALF OF GMAIL'S `step13rb`, and it can now do the same thing. Gmail labels the thread `AgentPilot/Handled` and step 1 excludes that label, so a door-handled thread is invisible to every later scan.

THIS USED TO MARK READ AND NOTHING ELSE, and the comment here admitted what that cost: 'an Outlook thread stays in scope until the scan window moves past it, so it may be classified again and spend another model call.' Read state was the closest thing available, and it is not a safe scan filter — the owner reads their own mail, so excluding read messages would hide a genuine unread reply the moment they glanced at it on a phone.

Graph categories are wired now. `AgentPilot/Handled` is a real mark that `step1` excludes through `exclude_categories`, so the thread is out of scope for good and the repeat classification is not paid for. The read flag stays because it is still correct on this branch — the client has their page and the owner has nothing left to do — but it carries no logic.

The branch exists in both plans because `oneAgentTwoMailboxes` requires it: the two must differ only in plumbing, and a missing step here is how one mailbox quietly grows behaviour the other does not have.

steps.name: Or close what the owner has already dealt with
steps.description: THE AGENT CLOSES ITS OWN CARD, because nothing else can. An owner answering a client does it in Outlook, which writes nothing to this platform — no send log row, no activity — so a card raised from a client's reply would sit there for ever, and a card you cannot clear is worse than never raising one. This agent is the only party that sees both sides: step 7 fetches the last thing sent to that client, and the model answers `already_handled` when it answers their question. Recording that is what lets the needs-you card stop returning them, by the same mechanism `enquiry_unanswered` already uses — a closing activity_type its find excludes.

steps.name: Record that they were answered
steps.description: Written every time the agent sees a settled thread, not only the first. A second row is harmless — the gap asks whether ANY exists — and the alternative is reading the timeline before writing, which costs a query per client to save a row nobody looks at twice.

steps.name: Mark it seen so it is not judged twice
steps.description: `already_handled` wrote an activity row and left nothing on the message, so the scan could not tell it had been judged. The watermark normally hides it, but not across the ten-minute overlap, not on a run started by hand, and not after a failed run - and a failed run retries up to five times, re-paying this classification each time. `AgentPilot/Seen` is the category `step1` excludes. It does not mark the message read: `step16` already does that for everything, and read state is deliberately not a scan filter.

steps.name: Or note that it needed nothing
steps.description: THE OUTCOME THAT LEFT NO TRACE AT ALL. `ignore` is the right answer for an out-of-office, a bounce or a bare thank-you, and it correctly writes no activity and shows the owner nothing - but it also left the message unmarked, so the agent could be asked to judge it again, at the full price of the classifier, in every case the watermark does not cover. This branch exists only to leave the mark; it writes nothing to the business and tells the owner nothing, which is what `ignore` means.

steps.name: Mark it seen
steps.description: The same category the other quiet outcome uses, for the same reason: `step1` excludes it, so a message judged not to need anybody is judged once.

else_steps.name: Is a person writing to us at all?
else_steps.description:
DROP THE MACHINES BEFORE A MODEL IS ASKED ANYTHING.

Nothing here costs a call: Gmail returns `labels` and the parsed sender on every scanned message, so these are string tests on data already in hand.

WHY IT EXISTS. Without it every stranger reached the triage, and a stranger is most of any inbox. Measured on one afternoon: 150 model calls and $1.05, of which 146 were triage — 97% of the spend asking a reasoning model whether a shoe-shop newsletter was a sales enquiry. A 48-hour window took 14 minutes to run. The triage is the one cost on this agent that scales with the SIZE of the mailbox rather than the size of the business, so it is the one that has to be defended.

Gmail's own category labels do most of the work, because Google has already sorted promotions, social and bulk updates out of the personal mail. The sender tests catch the rest: a no-reply address is nobody waiting for an answer, and our own sending domain is us talking to ourselves.

DELIBERATELY NOT A SPAM FILTER. Anything that survives still faces the triage, which is where judgement belongs. This only removes what needs no judgement at all.

steps.name: Is this a stranger worth knowing?
steps.description:
THE ONLY THING THAT READS A STRANGER, and it reads two lines of them.

Everything above this point ran on headers. This is the first judgement about somebody we have never written to, and it is made on the subject and the 200-character snippet that step 1 already returned — no body is fetched here, and none is fetched after it either. The owner opens the real message in their own inbox, which is where it already sits.

WHY IT COSTS A MODEL CALL AT ALL. No header separates a prospect from the accountant: both are real people writing real sentences from real addresses. The deterministic drops above catch machines, not humans. This is the price of covering first contact, and it is kept to a subject line and a snippet precisely because it is paid once per stranger — the one number on this agent that scales with the size of the mailbox.

NO MODEL IS NAMED HERE, AND THAT IS THE FIX RATHER THAN AN OMISSION. This step carried `model: gpt-5-nano`, pinned to stop the triage costing a dollar a run before the deterministic guard above existed. Two things were wrong with it. It breaks the platform rule against hardcoded model names (CLAUDE.md rule 5), and a nano model gets this particular judgement wrong — it filed a property mailshot as a lead for a parenting consultancy on 2026-11-10, because on a subject line and 200 characters a mailshot and an enquiry are separated only by DIRECTION.

Routing already answers it correctly: at this agent's AIS of 5.00 and a step complexity of 5.35 the effective score is 5.14, which lands in the balanced tier — `gpt-5.4-mini` under the current configuration. Measured, not assumed. So the override bought nothing the router was not already giving, and cost the one thing the router exists for: an operator can retune the tiers from the admin page and this step follows, where a pinned name would not.
steps.prompt:
You are the front desk of a small business, sorting the morning post.

This message is from an address this business has NEVER written to. You are
deciding one thing only: is a potential customer making contact?

You get the subject line and the first 200 characters. You do NOT get the body,
and you must not ask for it. A stranger's full message is not read unless you
say it is worth the owner's attention.

  from:    {{current_reply.from}}
  subject: {{current_reply.subject}}
  opening: {{current_reply.snippet}}

THE BUSINESS SELLS
{{service_list.rows}}

Answer 'yes' only when a HUMAN appears to be asking about what this business
sells, or about working with them. Examples: a price, availability, whether you
handle something, a request to be called back.

Answer 'no' for everything else, and most post is everything else: suppliers,
the accountant, the bank, a landlord, recruiters, cold sales approaches, anything
automated that slipped past the earlier checks, and anybody writing about a
subject this business does not sell.

THE TEST IS DIRECTION, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT GETS MISSED.

Ask which way the offer points: is this person trying to BUY what the business
sells, or to SELL something to the business? Anything OFFERING goods, services,
listings, properties, leads, candidates, finance, advertising, software, an
introduction or a free consultation is 'no' — however warmly it is written,
however personally it addresses the owner by name, and however plainly a real
human sent it.

A estate agent's listings, an agency's pitch, a recruiter's candidate and a
supplier's catalogue all arrive from a named person, addressed to the owner, in
the first person plural, inviting a call. Being addressed by name is not evidence
of an enquiry; it is evidence of a mailing list. 'Contact us for more
information' is somebody selling. 'Do you have anything on Tuesday' is somebody
buying.

Measured on this account, 2026-11-10: "Brickell Condos For Sale" — a property
mailshot opening "Hello Offir Omer, find below some recommended listings for you
… feel free to contact us" — was filed as a lead for a parenting-consultancy
business. Every surface fact said enquiry; only the direction said otherwise.

WHEN UNSURE, ANSWER 'no'. A missed enquiry is one message the owner reads in
their own inbox, where it already is. A wrong 'yes' files a stranger into their
customer list and asks them to deal with it, which is worse and harder to undo.

Write 'reason' in {{input.owner_language}}. It is shown on the owner's dashboard and nowhere else, so it follows the language THEY read, never the language the sender happened to use.

If the sender's own name is evident from the address or the From line, give it.
Never invent a name: leave it empty rather than guess.

steps.name: File them only if they are one
steps.description: The gate on the whole enquiry branch. A 'no' ends the message here having cost one small call and read nothing but a snippet.

steps.name: Add them to the contacts
steps.description:
FILED, NOT ANSWERED. The owner decided a stranger gets a contact and a flag, never a drafted reply: first contact sets the tone of a relationship, and the only business facts this agent holds are a list of service names.

The name may be absent — the triage step is told to leave it empty rather than invent one — so the address stands in for it. A contact called by their own email address is honest; one called by a guessed name is a mistake the owner has to find and correct.

steps.name: Flag it for the owner
steps.description:
THE FLAG IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THIS BRANCH. Without it a contact appears in the list with no explanation and the owner never learns a stranger wrote in — which is the gap this agent was widened to close.

The title carries their actual subject line and the description carries why the triage said yes, so the owner can judge the call without opening anything. `contact_id` comes from the row just created, which is why that step runs first.

steps.name: Flag the enquiry in the mailbox too
steps.description: A new enquiry is work waiting for the owner, which is what `AgentPilot/Needs you` already means on this mailbox, so a stranger worth knowing carries the same mark as a client question the agent would not answer. It is also what stops the triage being paid for twice: `step1` excludes this category.

else_steps.name: Mark a declined stranger seen
else_steps.description: THE MOST EXPENSIVE THING THE AGENT USED TO FORGET. A stranger the triage declines - a supplier, a recruiter, a cold approach - wrote nothing anywhere, so the next run judged them again, and judging a stranger is a MODEL CALL (`step5b`). This is the one cost on this agent that scales with the size of the mailbox rather than the size of the business, which is why it must not be paid twice for the same message. The category says only that this agent has looked: nothing is written to the business, no contact is created, and the owner is told nothing, because the triage said this is not a customer.

steps.name: Mark what it read as read
steps.description:
THE LAST THING DONE TO EVERY MESSAGE, WHATEVER WAS DECIDED ABOUT IT.

Outside the outcome branches on purpose. A drafted reply, an escalation, a thread judged already answered and a newsletter from a stranger were all READ by the agent, and the owner's inbox should say so for all four — otherwise the unread count keeps claiming work nobody still has to do.

Reading through the API does not change read state by itself, which is why this step has to exist: `messages.get` leaves UNREAD exactly as it found it, so without this the mailbox looks untouched no matter how much the agent processed.

WHAT THIS COSTS, SAID PLAINLY. An escalation goes read here, so the bold unread row is no longer what tells the owner a client is waiting. The card is, and in Gmail the label is. That is the trade the owner chose; it is reversible by setting `mark_read` to false, which puts UNREAD back.

Last in the scatter so it runs once per message and after every branch has had its say.
